result: The CPSF complex in T. gondii was biochemically characterized, with all subunits (CPSF1, CPSF2, CPSF3, CPSF4, Symplekin, Fip1, WDR33, PAP) displaying nuclear localization and being essential for parasite survival. CPSF1 immunoprecipitation followed by mass spectrometry identified the core CPSF complex subunits, with CPSF1 providing the most intact complex.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C67-C69, and C82 collectively demonstrate the composition and localization of the CPSF complex through immunofluorescence (C1, C67), mass spectrometry (C2, C3, C82), fitness assessment (C68), and expression profiling (C69). The data from multiple orthogonal approaches converge to support the characterization of the CPSF complex.

result: T. gondii CPSF4 has a unique architecture combining zinc fingers with a C-terminal YTH domain, a feature shared with plants but not with metazoa or fungi. This architecture is constitutively expressed in T. gondii throughout the life cycle, unlike the alternatively spliced plant isoforms.
evaluation: Claims C4-C8 and C70-C71 provide domain architecture analysis (C4, C5), evolutionary comparisons (C6), and expression data (C8) that collectively establish the unique CPSF4 architecture in T. gondii. The structural conservation with plants and divergence from metazoa/fungi is well-documented through sequence alignments and domain predictions.

result: The m6A writer complex in T. gondii consists of METTL3, METTL14, and WTAP, which display nuclear localization with punctate foci. METTL3 and METTL14 form a 400-500 kDa core complex, with METTL3 having an active catalytic site while METTL14 appears catalytically inactive. Two novel partners (TGME49_226660 and TGME49_275990) were identified.
evaluation: Claims C9-C12 and C46-C50 provide comprehensive characterization through immunofluorescence (C9, C10, C49), biochemical fractionation (C11, C12), sequence analysis (C47), and mass spectrometry (C50). The convergence of localization, biochemical, and sequence data strongly supports the composition and properties of the m6A writer complex.

result: Depletion of METTL3 using the auxin-inducible degron system results in a significant reduction in m6A levels, with effects detectable at 12 hr and more dramatic at 24 hr. The m6A mark is predominantly cytoplasmic in tachyzoites.
evaluation: Claims C13-C16 demonstrate the functional role of METTL3 through controlled depletion experiments (C13), localization of m6A (C14), and quantification of m6A levels by both immunofluorescence and ELISA (C15, C16). The time-course data and orthogonal validation methods provide strong support.

result: The YTH domains of T. gondii CPSF4 and Arabidopsis thaliana CPSF30 specifically bind m6A-modified RNA with dissociation constants of 5.05 ± 0.44 μM and 0.33 ± 0.03 μM, respectively, showing no binding to unmodified RNA.
evaluation: Claims C17-C19 provide quantitative ITC measurements demonstrating specific m6A binding for both T. gondii and A. thaliana YTH domains. The specificity is established by the lack of binding to unmodified RNA (C18), and the comparative data supports evolutionary conservation of function despite differences in affinity.

result: The crystal structure of T. gondii CPSF4-YTH domain in complex with m6A-modified RNA was determined at 1.45 Å resolution, revealing a well-structured domain with six alpha helices and five beta sheets. The m6A-binding site involves residues near helices α1/α2/α3 and beta sheet 1, with 38% sequence identity to human YTHDC1.
evaluation: Claims C20-C25 provide high-resolution structural data (C20) with detailed description of secondary structure elements (C21, C22), conformational analysis (C23), and comparative structural analysis (C24, C25). The 1.45 Å resolution provides high confidence in the structural details, and the comparison to YTHDC1 establishes evolutionary relationships.

result: Depletion of CPSF4 results in transcriptional readthrough beyond annotated 3' ends, generating elongated transcripts. Nanopore DRS data indicate that the proximal polyadenylation site is overrun and an alternative downstream PAS is used.
evaluation: Claims C26-C27 demonstrate transcriptional readthrough through both Illumina RNA-seq (C26) and nanopore DRS (C27). The nanopore data provides direct evidence of full-length polyadenylated transcripts extending beyond canonical 3' ends, supporting the mechanism of PAS overrun and alternative site usage.

result: Depletion of METTL3 phenocopies CPSF4 depletion in generating transcriptional readthrough chimeric RNAs, with most readthrough events in METTL3 KD also found in CPSF4 KD. CPSF4 shows a higher number of readthrough events, and chimera formation occurs globally across all chromosomes.
evaluation: Claims C28-C31 provide comparative analysis of METTL3 and CPSF4 knockdowns using nanopore DRS and ChimerID analysis. The overlap in readthrough events (C29), genome-wide distribution (C31), and mechanistic explanation for differences (C30) collectively support the functional link between m6A deposition and CPSF4-mediated polyadenylation.

result: In Arabidopsis thaliana, nanopore DRS confirmed the existence of full-length chimeric transcripts in fip37L and cpsf30-3 mutants, caused by readthrough of upstream genes that fail to terminate and instead terminate at the PAS of adjacent genes.
evaluation: Claims C32-C33 provide direct evidence from nanopore DRS in plant mutants, demonstrating that the m6A-dependent polyadenylation mechanism is conserved between T. gondii and plants. The single-molecule sequencing approach provides unambiguous evidence of full-length chimeric transcripts.

result: Using differential error analysis of nanopore DRS data, putative m6A sites were identified with an enriched motif ARACW (resembling the RGAC consensus). About 65% of error sites mapped to the RRAC motif, with m6A sites located mostly in 3'UTRs and at sites where proximal PAS are overrun.
evaluation: Claims C34-C37 use the Epinano pipeline to identify m6A sites through differential error rates between WT and METTL3 KD samples. The motif enrichment (C34), quantification (C35), localization (C36), and association with termination defects (C37) provide convergent evidence for m6A site identification and functional relevance.

result: Genes targeted by readthrough following CPSF4 and METTL3 KD are developmentally regulated genes adjacent to expressed tachyzoite genes. The readthrough phenotype is specific to CPSF4/METTL3 KD and not observed in MORC KD, which shows conventional promoter-dependent upregulation. This suggests m6A-dependent polyadenylation serves as a transcriptional barrier for developmental gene regulation.
evaluation: Claims C38-C45 provide comprehensive analysis of the biological function of m6A-dependent polyadenylation. The characterization of target genes (C38, C39, C42), comparison with MORC KD as a control (C40), and detailed analysis of specific loci like ROP35 (C42-C45) collectively support the proposed mechanism. The nanopore data distinguishes readthrough from conventional upregulation.

result: The m6A mark in T. gondii appears to have a relatively long half-life and low dynamism, consistent with the absence of m6A demethylases in Apicomplexa. This contrasts with human cells where m6A content falls by ~75% only after 96 hr following triple knockdown of METTL3, METTL14, and WTAP.
evaluation: Claims C51, C52, and C61 integrate observations from T. gondii knockdown kinetics (C15) with comparative data from human cells (C51) and phylogenetic analysis (C52) to support the inference about m6A stability. The absence of erasers (C52) provides a mechanistic explanation for the observed stability.

result: The N-terminal zinc finger domains of CPSF4 show partial conservation, suggesting the PAS motif may have diverged. The YTH domain is separated from zinc fingers by a predicted disordered region that may be involved in phase separation, and a potential secondary binding groove suggests multiple RNA binding modes.
evaluation: Claims C53-C56 are largely speculative (C53, C54) or based on predictions (C55) and citations (C56). While the structural observations are valid, the functional implications regarding PAS motif divergence (C53) and multiple binding modes (C54) require experimental validation. The speculation is reasonable but not directly tested.

result: An m6A-dependent polyadenylation mechanism exists in T. gondii where m6A guides the polyadenylation machinery via CPSF4 YTH binding. This mechanism is detected mainly at tachyzoite-specific genes adjacent to repressed developmental genes, and the differential expression of m6A enzymes and 3' processing factors across life stages supports stage-specific requirements.
evaluation: Claims C57-C60 synthesize the mechanistic model from the experimental data. The proposed mechanism (C57) is supported by the biochemical binding data (C17-C19), structural data (C20-C25), and functional genomics (C26-C45). The localization to specific genomic contexts (C58) and expression patterns (C60) provide additional support, though C59 is somewhat speculative.

result: In Arabidopsis thaliana, m6A-dependent polyadenylation serves to prevent aberrant transcription at rearranged loci. Despite functional conservation between plants and T. gondii, evolutionary divergence drove each organism to evolve this mechanism for their respective needs.
evaluation: Claims C62-C63 are well-supported by citations to Parker et al., 2020 and Pontier et al., 2019, and are corroborated by the authors' own nanopore data (C32-C33). Claim C64 is interpretive but reasonable given the data. The evolutionary argument is supported by the conservation of CPSF4 architecture and functional similarities.

result: Nanopore DRS revealed genome assembly artifacts and mis-annotated or non-annotated loci in the T. gondii genome.
evaluation: Claim C65 is explicitly stated and supported by the nanopore DRS data, which provides long-read information that can identify assembly errors and annotation issues. This is a technical observation that validates the utility of the nanopore approach.

result: The m6A modification has been linked to translational potential and stability of transcripts in Plasmodium falciparum, raising questions about whether m6A/polyadenylation coupling serves similar functions in transcriptional partitioning in this parasite.
evaluation: Claim C66 is primarily speculative, citing prior work in P. falciparum (Baumgarten et al., 2019) and raising questions about functional conservation. While the speculation is reasonable given the conservation of CPSF4 architecture, no direct experimental evidence is provided for P. falciparum.

result: The PAP enzyme was not detected in most CPSF immunoprecipitations except for weak amounts in WDR33 interactome, possibly due to transient binding or disruption during stringent washing conditions.
evaluation: Claims C72-C73 report a negative result (C72) with a reasonable mechanistic explanation (C73). The observation is clearly stated and the speculation about transient binding or weak interactions is appropriately qualified. This is a technical observation relevant to understanding CPSF complex dynamics.

result: Apicomplexan and plant species share many protein architectures due to an early algae-related endosymbiotic event, exemplified by plant-like AP2 factors with high regulatory potential in apicomplexans.
evaluation: Claims C74-C75 provide evolutionary context for the shared CPSF4 architecture. C74 is established knowledge about endosymbiosis, and C75 provides a specific example with citation (Jeninga et al., 2019). This contextualizes the main findings within established evolutionary biology.

result: Prior work in animals and plants has shown connections between m6A and polyadenylation, including opposing effects on APA site choice in animals, methylation of PAS motifs in plants, and generation of chimeric mRNAs in CPSF30-YTH deficient plants.
evaluation: Claims C76-C79 summarize prior literature with appropriate citations (Kasowitz et al., 2018; Yue et al., 2018; Parker et al., 2020; Pontier et al., 2019). These claims establish the context for the current work and are well-supported by the cited literature.

result: The overall architecture of the CPSF complex in Apicomplexa was debated prior to this study, with only bioinformatics-based identification of subunits and no direct biochemical evidence for protein interactions in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C80-C81 establish the knowledge gap that this study addresses. The claims are appropriately qualified and cite prior bioinformatics work (Ospina-Villa et al., 2020; Stevens et al., 2018), setting up the novelty of the biochemical characterization presented.

result: Two unknown proteins (TGME49_261960 with RNA recognition motif and TGME49_254210 with C2H2 zinc finger) were detected in CPSF1 immunoprecipitation and may be apicomplexan-specific CPSF/CSTF subunits. The poor peptide coverage of Fip1 may be due to degradation of this mostly unstructured protein.
evaluation: Claims C83-C84 report interesting observations from mass spectrometry but are speculative about function (C83) and mechanism (C84). The identification of novel interactors is supported by the data, but their functional roles as CPSF/CSTF subunits require further validation. The explanation for Fip1 is reasonable but speculative.
